entry: Self-propulsion and gliding across a flat ice surface on metal-bladed skates. People skate for recreation, exercise, competition and commuting, on naturally frozen ponds, lakes, canals and rivers as well as on indoor and outdoor rinks. Ancient skates made of animal bones were found at the Gaotai Ruins in northwest [[China]], estimated to be 3,500 years old. True skating began when steel blades with sharpened edges came into use, and the [[Netherlands|Dutch]] added edges to skates in the 13th or 14th century. Metal skates seem to have reached England with the Restoration in 1660. [[Ice hockey]], bandy and ringette are team sports; [[Figure skating]] and [[Speed skating]] are individual disciplines, and synchronized skating is an artistic team sport derived from figure skating.

Large piece of fresh water ice, more than 15 m (16 yards) long, broken off a glacier or ice shelf and floating freely in open water. Much of an iceberg lies below the water's surface, a fact behind the phrase "tip of the iceberg." Typically about one-tenth of an iceberg's volume is above water, following from Archimedes's principle of buoyancy. Icebergs calving from [[Glacier|glaciers]] in [[Greenland]] are often irregularly shaped, while [[Antarctica|Antarctic]] ice shelves produce large tabular icebergs. The largest on record, a tabular iceberg measuring 335 by 97 km (208 by 60 mi), was sighted by the USS Glacier on November 12, 1956, and was larger than [[Belgium]]. Icebergs are a serious maritime hazard, and smaller fragments are called growlers or bergy bits.

Nordic island country between the Arctic Ocean and the North Atlantic Ocean. It is Europe's westernmost and most sparsely populated country. Its capital, [[Reykjavík]], is home to about 35% of its roughly 395,000 residents. The interior is a volcanic plateau with sand and lava fields, mountains and glaciers, and the island has [[Geyser|geysers]] and frequent volcanic eruptions. Settlement began in 874 AD, and the Althing, one of the world's oldest functioning legislative assemblies, governed an independent commonwealth. Iceland acceded to [[Norway|Norwegian]] rule in the 13th century and came under de facto Danish rule from 1523. Under the 1918 Danish–Icelandic Act of Union it became a kingdom sharing the Danish monarch; it voted overwhelmingly to become a republic in 1944. It joined the [[Council of Europe]] in 1950. It has the smallest population of any [[NATO]] member and is the only one with no standing army.

Religious work of art, most commonly a [[Painting|painting]], in the cultures of Eastern Orthodox, Oriental Orthodox, Catholic and Lutheran churches. The most common subjects are Jesus, Mary, saints and angels, though the term also covers narrative scenes from the Bible or the lives of saints. Icons are most often painted on wood panels with egg tempera, but may be cast in metal, carved in stone, embroidered on cloth or made as [[Mosaic|mosaic]] or fresco. The Greek term for icon painting is the same word as for "writing," so Orthodox sources often call it icon writing. Eastern Orthodox tradition holds that Christian images date to the earliest days of Christianity, while academic art history traces the tradition back only to the 3rd century. Widespread destruction of images during the Byzantine Iconoclasm of 726–842 settled permanently the question of their appropriateness. Since then, icons have shown great continuity of style and subject.

Destruction of icons, images or monuments, often for religious or political reasons. It is most common in religions opposed to idolatry, such as the [[Abrahamic religions]], and more often arises from disputes between factions of the same religion than between faiths. In Egypt during the Amarna Period, [[Akhenaten]] ordered the eradication of traditional gods, and many temples and monuments were destroyed. The [[Hebrew Bible]] records God instructing the Israelites to destroy the engraved stones and molded images of the Canaanites. Protestant reformers such as [[John Calvin]] condemned images as violations of the Second Commandment, and in 1566 mobs in the Netherlands destroyed altarpieces, statues and crucifixes. The term originates from struggles over religious icons in the [[Byzantine Empire|Byzantine]] Empire from 726 to 842 AD. Outside religion, it has included destruction of monarchist symbols during the [[French Revolution]].

Family of small to medium-sized, often colorful, New World [[Passerine|passerine]] birds, also called New World blackbirds. The family Icteridae has 108 species in 30 genera, and most have black as the predominant plumage color, often enlivened by yellow, orange or red. The name means "jaundiced ones," from the yellow feathers of many species. The family includes orioles, the bobolink, meadowlarks, grackles, cowbirds, oropendolas and caciques. Most species live in the tropics, with the highest breeding densities in [[Colombia]] and southern [[Mexico]]. Icterids often display considerable [[Sexual dimorphism|sexual dimorphism]]; the male great-tailed grackle is 60% heavier than the female. Many species nest in colonies of up to 100,000 birds, and some cowbirds lay their eggs in other species' nests, as some [[Cuckoo|cuckoos]] do. Red-winged blackbirds are considered the worst vertebrate pests on some crops, such as [[Rice|rice]], in the United States.

Three agents of the psyche in the structural model of [[Sigmund Freud]]. Freud introduced the model in *Beyond the Pleasure Principle* (1920) and refined it in *The Ego and the Id* (1923). The id is the unconscious source of instinctual needs and desires, governed by the pleasure principle. The superego is the internalized set of social rules and norms, largely shaped by parental demands in childhood. The ego mediates between the id's energies, external reality and the superego's constraints. The terms are Latinizations by translator James Strachey; Freud wrote *das Es*, *das Ich* and *das Über-Ich*.

British-born American actress and filmmaker. Lupino appeared in 59 films during a 48-year career and directed eight. She worked mainly in the United States, becoming a citizen in 1948. She was the first woman to direct a film noir, *The Hitch-Hiker* (1953), and through her independent company she co-wrote and co-produced social-message films. Her directed films include *Not Wanted* (1949), about unwed pregnancy, and *Outrage* (1950), one of the first films about rape. *Never Fear* (1950) was loosely based on her own experiences with [[Polio|polio]]. As an actress she starred in *High Sierra* (1941) with [[Humphrey Bogart]]. She also directed more than 100 television episodes and was the only woman to direct an episode of *The Twilight Zone*. Her directing career is a pioneering example of proto-feminist filmmaking.

Landlocked U.S. state in the Pacific Northwest and Mountain West. Its capital and largest city is Boise, and its population is approximately two million. Idaho is the 14th-largest state by land area and is quite mountainous, containing several stretches of the [[Rocky Mountains]]. The U.S. Forest Service holds about 38% of its land. Idaho was admitted to the Union on July 3, 1890, as the 43rd state. Its [[Potato|potato]] crop, about one-third of the nationwide yield, is its best-known product. It has been a predominantly [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican]] state since statehood.

Equation of state of a hypothetical ideal gas, written pV = nRT. Also called the general gas equation, it combines [[Boyle's law]], Charles's law, Avogadro's law and Gay-Lussac's law. Benoît Paul Émile Clapeyron and, independently, Dmitry Mendeleev first stated it in 1834. The variables are [[Pressure|pressure]] p, volume V, [[Temperature|temperature]] T and amount of substance n, with R the ideal gas constant, 8.314 J/(mol·K). In SI units, p is measured in [[Pascal (unit)|pascals]], V in cubic meters, n in [[Mole (unit)|moles]] and T in [[Kelvin|kelvins]]. The law can also be derived from kinetic theory. It is a good approximation for many gases under many conditions, but real gases deviate at high pressures or low temperatures.

Set of metaphysical positions holding that consciousness or spirit is the most fundamental reality. Indian philosophy contains early defenses of idealism in [[Vedanta]] and Shaiva Pratyabhijña thought, and the [[Mahayana]] Yogācāra school argued for a "mind-only" philosophy. In the West, idealism traces to [[Plato]], who held that timeless ideas constitute the highest reality. [[Immanuel Kant]]'s transcendental idealism argued that knowledge of reality is based on mental structures. [[George Berkeley]] held that physical objects are collections of ideas in perceiving minds. Idealism is contrasted with [[Materialism|materialism]] and realism. Critics including G. E. Moore and [[Bertrand Russell]] attacked it from analytic philosophy, but many of its aspects still influence philosophy.

Qualities, beliefs, personality traits, appearance or expressions that characterize a person or group. Identity is shaped by social and cultural factors and by how others perceive a person, and it emerges during childhood. In sociology, the emphasis is on collective identity, the group memberships that define a person and guide behavior. In psychology, the term usually refers to personal identity, the distinctive traits that make an individual unique, and it is strongly associated with self-concept and [[Self-esteem|self-esteem]]. [[Erik Erikson]] was among the earliest psychologists to study identity, and he saw its conflict as arising mainly in [[Adolescence|adolescence]]. Social identity theory, developed by Henri Tajfel and John Turner in the 1970s, holds that people favor their in-groups to bolster self-esteem.

Use of another person's personal identifying information, without permission, to commit fraud or other crimes. The term was coined in 1964 and has been legally defined in both the U.K. and the U.S. as the theft of personally identifiable information. Such information includes a name, date of birth, Social Security number, bank account or credit card numbers, PINs, [[Fingerprint|fingerprints]] and [[Password|passwords]]. Victims often do not know how their information was obtained, and a data breach does not always lead to identity theft; a U.S. Government Accountability Office study found that "most breaches have not resulted in detected incidents of identity theft." Identity theft may facilitate or fund other crimes, including [[Terrorism|terrorism]], [[Phishing|phishing]] and [[Espionage|espionage]]. In 2024 the Federal Trade Commission recorded over 1.1 million identity theft complaints.

Ugandan military officer and dictator, president of [[Uganda]] (1971–1979). Amin served in the British colonial King's African Rifles from 1946 and rose to command the Ugandan army. In 1971 he overthrew Milton Obote in a [[Coup d'état|coup]], after learning that Obote planned to arrest him. His regime was marked by rampant human rights abuses, economic mismanagement and corruption. International observers and human rights groups estimate that between 100,000 and 500,000 people were killed under his rule. In 1972 he expelled Asians, most of them Indian-Ugandans, and [[India]] severed diplomatic relations. Amin attempted to annex Tanzania's Kagera Region in 1978; the [[Tanzania|Tanzanian]] army invaded Uganda and captured [[Kampala]] in 1979. He went into exile in Libya, Iraq and finally [[Saudi Arabia]], where he lived until his death.

American actress, singer and songwriter. She rose to prominence in *[[Rent (musical)|Rent]]* in 1996, and in 2003 she originated the role of Elphaba in *[[Wicked (musical)|Wicked]]* on Broadway, winning the Tony Award for Best Actress in a Musical. Since 2013 she has voiced Elsa in Disney's *Frozen* franchise, and "Let It Go" won the Academy Award for Best Original Song. Menzel has released seven studio albums; *Holiday Wishes* (2014) is her highest-charting, peaking at number six on the Billboard 200.

Worship of an idol as though it were a deity. The term is often associated with Abrahamic religions such as [[Judaism]], [[Christianity]] and [[Islam]], which forbid it in texts such as the [[Ten Commandments]]. The definition of idolatry is contested within these faiths; many Muslims and most Protestant Christians condemn the veneration of the Virgin Mary practiced in Catholic and Eastern Orthodox churches as idolatry. In [[Hinduism]], [[Buddhism]] and [[Jainism]], cult images known as murti serve as symbols of the divine and as aids to worship (bhakti). The word comes from the Ancient Greek *eidololatria*, meaning "worship of idols." The opposition to images is called aniconism, and their destruction is called [[Iconoclasm|iconoclasm]].

English actor, DJ, rapper and producer. He is known for playing Stringer Bell in *The Wire* and DCI John Luther in the BBC series *Luther*, which earned him a Golden Globe Award. He played Heimdall in six films of the [[Marvel Cinematic Universe]] and portrayed [[Nelson Mandela]] in *Mandela: Long Walk to Freedom* (2013). He voiced Chief Bogo in *Zootopia* and Knuckles the Echidna in the *Sonic the Hedgehog* films. He made his directorial debut with *Yardie* (2018) and performs as a DJ under the name DJ Big Driis.

Niger–Congo language, the principal native language of the [[Igbo people]] in southeastern [[Nigeria]]. The core Igbo cluster is generally thought to be one language, though its northern, western, southern and eastern groupings have limited mutual intelligibility. A standard literary form, *Igbo izugbe*, was adopted around 1972. Igbo is tonal, and words may differ only in tone: *ákwá* means "cry" and *àkwà* means "bed." The language was spoken by many enslaved people trafficked to the Americas during the [[Atlantic slave trade]]. Igbo is the dominant language in the Nigerian states of Abia, Anambra, Ebonyi, Enugu, Imo and Northern Delta. [[Chinua Achebe]] criticized the language standardization efforts in a 1999 lecture.

Ethnic group of southeastern [[Nigeria]], one of the largest in Africa. The Igbo language belongs to the Niger–Congo family. Before British colonial rule, the Igbo were largely governed by centralized chiefdoms such as Nri, the Aro Confederacy, Onitsha and Nnewi. The Igbo became overwhelmingly [[Christianity|Christian]] during the colonial era. After Nigeria's independence in 1960, the Igbo seceded and attempted to establish Biafra, triggering the [[Nigerian Civil War]] (1967–1970). Millions of Biafran civilians died of starvation during a blockade, and Biafra was eventually reintegrated into Nigeria. Igbo communities also live in [[Cameroon]], [[Gabon]] and Equatorial Guinea.

Dome-shaped shelter built of blocks of [[Snow|snow]]. Traditionally, igloos were built by the [[Inuit]] of Canada's Central Arctic and in the Qaanaaq area of [[Greenland]]. They served as temporary shelters on hunting trips or, in larger forms, as semi-permanent family dwellings. Snow insulates because of the air trapped in it, so inside temperatures may range from −7 to 16 °C (19 to 61 °F) when warmed by body heat alone, even when outside temperatures fall to −45 °C (−49 °F). Snow igloos are built in a catenary curve rather than a sphere, and the largest could have up to five rooms and house 20 people. Igloo building has declined in modern times, but it is still taught for heritage preservation in some Inuit communities.

Spanish Catholic priest and theologian, co-founder of the [[Jesuits|Society of Jesus]]. A former soldier, Ignatius envisioned the society's purpose as missionary work and teaching. With six companions he founded the society and became its first Superior General. In addition to the usual vows of chastity, obedience and poverty, he added a fourth vow of obedience to the pope for projects the pontiff ordains. Jesuits were instrumental in leading the [[Counter-Reformation]]. His *Spiritual Exercises* (1548) gave rise to Ignatian spirituality. He was canonized as a saint in 1622, and he is the patron saint of the Basque provinces of Gipuzkoa and Biscay, as well as of the Society of Jesus.

Hungarian physician of German descent and early pioneer of antiseptic procedures. In 1847 Semmelweis proposed hand washing with chlorinated lime solutions at the First Obstetrical Clinic of Vienna General Hospital, where doctors' wards had thrice the mortality of midwives' wards. The maternal mortality rate dropped from 18% to less than 2%. He published his findings in *Etiology, Concept and Prophylaxis of Childbed Fever* in 1861. Many in the medical community rejected his ideas, in part because he could not offer a theoretical explanation for them. He was committed to an asylum in 1865 and died 14 days later from a gangrenous wound. His findings gained acceptance after [[Louis Pasteur]] confirmed the germ theory of disease and [[Joseph Lister]] pioneered antiseptic surgery.

Rock formed by the cooling and solidification of [[Magma|magma]] or [[Lava|lava]]. It is one of the three main rock types, alongside [[Sedimentary rock|sedimentary]] and [[Metamorphic rock|metamorphic]] rock. Intrusive igneous rocks cool slowly underground and are coarse-grained, as in [[Granite|granite]] and gabbro. Extrusive, or volcanic, rocks form rapidly at or near the surface and are fine-grained or glassy; [[Basalt|basalt]] is the most common. Igneous and metamorphic rocks make up 90–95% of the top 16 km (9.9 mi) of Earth's crust by volume. Igneous rocks form about 15% of Earth's current land surface and most of the oceanic crust. Tungsten, tin and uranium are commonly associated with granites, while chromium and platinum are associated with gabbros.

Russian-born composer and conductor, a pivotal figure in modernist music. Born into a musical family, he studied law at the University of Saint Petersburg before studying music with [[Nikolai Rimsky-Korsakov]] until 1908. Sergei Diaghilev commissioned him to write three [[Ballet|ballets]] for the Ballets Russes's Paris seasons: *The Firebird* (1910), *Petrushka* (1911) and *The Rite of Spring* (1913). The premiere of *The Rite of Spring* caused a near-riot, and its unusual technique influenced composers' understanding of rhythmic structure. His career is often divided into Russian (1913–1920), neoclassical (1920–1951) and serial (1954–1968) periods. In the neoclassical period he drew on Greek mythology in *Oedipus rex* (1927) and *Persephone* (1935). In the serial period he adopted the twelve-tone technique of [[Arnold Schoenberg]], beginning with *In Memoriam Dylan Thomas* (1954). He became a French citizen in 1934 and an American citizen in 1945.

Genus of large, bulky herbivorous iguanodontian [[Dinosaur|dinosaurs]] of the Early [[Cretaceous]]. Named in 1825 by Gideon Mantell from fossils found in England, it was the second dinosaur formally named, after *Megalosaurus*. Modern revision defines the genus by *I. bernissartensis*, which lived in [[Belgium]], Germany, Spain and possibly England, between about 126 and 122 million years ago. It measured up to 9–11 m (30–36 ft) in length and 4.5 metric tons (5.0 short tons) in body mass. Its large thumb spikes were possibly used against predators, and its long prehensile fifth fingers could forage for food. Remains discovered in Belgium in 1878 revealed its anatomy in unprecedented detail. As one of the first well-known dinosaurs, it has had a notable place in the public's perception of dinosaurs.
